summary: Describes Lemonade, a profile of IMAP, mail submission and Sieve that helps constrained clients, such as mobile devices with limited memory or bandwidth, use email efficiently. It lists required extensions, restrictions and usage modes.

plainLanguage.summary: Phones have small screens and slow connections. This note picks a set of email features that make mail work well on those devices.

questions: how to make imap efficient on mobile devices

which imap extensions does lemonade require
subtitle: A checklist of IMAP, mail submission and Sieve extensions that lets phones and other constrained clients handle email cheaply.

tldr.problem: Email clients on devices with little memory, bandwidth or processing power, or on flaky networks, pay a high price for ordinary IMAP and SMTP submission: downloading mail just to forward it, re-synchronizing whole mailboxes after a dropped connection, and extra round trips.
tldr.mechanism: The Lemonade profile does not invent a new protocol. It lists which existing IMAP, submission and Sieve extensions servers MUST support, adds one new IMAP capability (URL-PARTIAL) and two keywords, and describes how clients use them, including forwarding without downloading.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4550 and adds more required extensions for message stores and delivery agents. Any ordinary IMAP client still works, but constrained clients can take full advantage of the profile.

facts.label: Submission port
facts.value: 587 (clients MUST use it unless configured otherwise)

today: RFC 5550 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4550 and updates RFC 4469 and RFC 4467. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Lemonade Profile Is
sections.content:
The Lemonade Profile is a set of required extensions, restrictions and usage modes layered on three existing protocols: IMAP, mail submission and Sieve. It is aimed at clients that are constrained in memory, bandwidth, processing power or other ways.

A Lemonade mail server provides a Lemonade Submission Server and a Lemonade Message Store, based on the existing submission protocol and IMAP respectively. It MAY also include a Lemonade Message Delivery Agent that filters mail at delivery time using Sieve.

The profile covers general enhancements to Internet mail, forwarding without download, quick mailbox resynchronization, richer notifications and view filters from the store, and delivery-time filtering. The text says it is intended to support realizations of the Open Mobile Alliance's mobile email enabler using IETF Internet Mail protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Lemonade is not a new kind of email. It is a list of extra email tricks that a mail server should know, so small devices can use email without wasting time and data.

sections.title: Three Roles and Their Required Support
sections.content:
Section 3 summarizes what each role MUST support, in tables that point at the sections giving details.

  • A Submission Server MUST provide the service of the submission protocol and support these SMTP extensions: 8BITMIME, AUTH, BINARYMIME, BURL (with the imap option), CHUNKING, DSN, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, PIPELINING, SIZE and STARTTLS.
  • A Message Store MUST provide IMAP and support a longer list that includes BINARY, CATENATE, COMPRESS=DEFLATE, CONDSTORE, CONTEXT=SEARCH, CONTEXT=SORT, CONVERT, ENABLE, ESEARCH, ESORT, I18NLEVEL=1, IDLE, LITERAL+, NAMESPACE, NOTIFY, QRESYNC, SASL-IR, SORT, STARTTLS, UIDPLUS, URLAUTH and URL-PARTIAL, plus the $Forwarded, $SubmitPending and $Submitted keywords. It MUST also send the CAPABILITY response code in the initial greeting and after LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE.
  • A Message Delivery Agent MUST support Sieve and the ENOTIFY, IMAP4FLAGS, RELATIONAL, VACATION and VARIABLES extensions, plus the i;unicode-casemap comparator.

Delivery agents should also consider supporting a Sieve script management protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of three helpers in a post office: one who sends letters, one who keeps your mailbox, and one who sorts mail as it arrives. Each helper gets its own checklist of skills.

sections.title: Submission Server Requirements
sections.content:
Every Lemonade Submission Server is a normal mail submission server, so any client that submits mail the usual way still works. The extra extensions exist to make submission efficient.

  • Forward without download: servers MUST support BURL, 8BITMIME, BINARYMIME and CHUNKING, and BURL MUST support URLAUTH-type URLs, so the server advertises the imap option after the BURL keyword.
  • Pipelining: MUST be supported, because mobile or satellite networks have high latency and skipping round trips saves both bandwidth and total time.
  • Delivery status notifications: MUST be supported.
  • Message size declaration: MUST be supported so failures show up early. The server MUST expand all BURL parts before judging whether the size is acceptable. A client MUST NOT send a message it knows exceeds the advertised maximum, and the size it declares in MAIL FROM MUST be at least the size of the assembled message.
  • Enhanced status codes: MUST be supported, so a client can find the precise cause of failure.
  • TLS: secure SMTP over TLS MUST be supported. DEFLATE compression for TLS is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending helper must be able to take instructions in a batch, say exactly why a letter failed, refuse a parcel that is too big before you carry it over, and use a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Message Store Requirements
sections.content:
A Lemonade Message Store is an IMAP server, so any IMAP client works with it. It adds extensions that address the limits of some clients and networks.

  • Quick resynchronization: CONDSTORE, QRESYNC and ENABLE MUST be supported. A client can ask for all flag changes and expunges since a previously recorded state, which also speeds up reconnecting after the transport is cut. Clients and servers implementing QRESYNC need to follow the errata listed in Appendix A.
  • Message parts: BINARY MUST be supported, moving MIME body part decoding from client to server. Servers SHALL always accept binary-encoded MIME messages in APPEND. CONVERT MUST also be supported, so clients can request conversions such as scaling images.
  • Compression: servers SHOULD support DEFLATE for TLS, but MUST support COMPRESS=DEFLATE as an application-level fallback, because TLS compression is rarely deployed on many endpoints.
  • Notifications: IDLE MUST be supported and its notifications sent in a timely manner. NOTIFY lets clients request specific event types, such as message delivery and mailbox renames, for the selected folder and others.
  • Searching and views: ESEARCH, CONTEXT=SEARCH, ESORT, CONTEXT=SORT and SORT MUST be supported, so a client can work with a view of a mailbox instead of the whole thing.
  • Mailbox handling and extras: NAMESPACE, I18NLEVEL (value 1 or 2), LITERAL+ and SASL-IR MUST be supported, and IMAP over TLS is required.
sections.plainLanguage: The mailbox keeper must be good at three things: quickly telling you only what changed while you were away, shrinking big parcels, and tapping you on the shoulder the moment new mail comes in.

sections.title: Delivery Agents and Mail Clients
sections.content:
Delivery agents MUST support Sieve at the point of delivery, so the user controls which messages are accepted and where they are filed. The required Sieve extensions each have a stated job: VACATION sets up an auto-responder, ENOTIFY lets a script generate notifications (such as XMPP, SIP or email), VARIABLES adds variables, RELATIONAL adds relational comparisons, IMAP4FLAGS sets IMAP flags on delivery, and i;unicode-casemap gives case-insensitive matching of Unicode characters. If an agent supports the ManageSieve protocol, it MUST advertise all of these extensions there.

All existing IMAP clients are already Lemonade compliant, since the services are built on IMAP and submission. Client authors are encouraged to use the extra facilities. Clients MUST connect to the submission server on port 587 unless configured otherwise, and MAY retry on a different port such as 25 if that fails. Clients SHOULD support the Format and DelSp parameters of text/plain and generate that format, and SHOULD support and use the $Forwarded keyword.
sections.plainLanguage: The sorting helper follows your rules, like putting mail from Grandma in a special box or replying that you are away. Your own app should knock on the right door (port 587) when sending mail.

sections.title: Forward Without Download
sections.content:
Client/server email turned local disk operations into repeated network transfers. In the traditional strategy the client assembles the whole message itself, so saving a draft, fetching it again and submitting it each move the entire, possibly large, content.

Lemonade avoids this by combining the BURL extension with IMAP URLAUTH. The client asks the IMAP server for an authorized URL, and the submission server fetches the referenced content straight from the IMAP server. Because the details stay in the submission server, the approach works with other retrieval protocols such as POP or NNTP too, and the client keeps using one submission protocol.

The RFC describes two ways to do this, depending on where message assembly happens:

  • IMAP CATENATE: the client uses an extended APPEND to build the message on the IMAP server from new text plus existing parts, learns its UID through UIDPLUS, requests a URL with GENURLAUTH, and hands that URL to the submission server with BURL. This suits cases where a copy should stay on the IMAP server.
  • SMTP CHUNKING and BURL: the client sends new data with BDAT commands and refers to existing parts with BURL, and the submission server assembles the message.

In both, the client may then set the $Forwarded keyword on the original message, which the RFC calls non-critical and omittable. The secure link relies on a "pawn-ticket": a URL carrying its own authorization credentials. It gives the submission server access only to the specific data it is authorized for, can be revoked by the client, and can have a time-limited validity.

For copies of sent messages (the "fcc problem"), the final message can be appended to the outgoing-mail mailbox, using the $SubmitPending and $Submitted keywords. APPEND creates only a single copy, and more copies on the same server can be made with COPY.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine mailing a friend a photo that is already in an album at the post office. Instead of taking it home and bringing it back, you hand the clerk a signed slip saying "use that photo". The slip only works for that clerk and that photo.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC mostly points implementors at the security sections of every referenced document and adds a few combination-specific notes. The mandatory-to-implement authentication mechanism for submission is in the SMTP AUTH document, and for IMAP it is in the IMAP specification.

Using BURL is no riskier than sending the text directly, even without TLS: without BURL an eavesdropper sees the full text, and with BURL they may or may not, depending on the form of BURL used. Still, the URLAUTH token sent to the submission server should be protected from interception to avoid a replay attack that could disclose the message. TLS on both the IMAP session that issues GENURLAUTH and the submission path protects against this.

Submission servers SHOULD use TLS-protected IMAP connections when fetching content with the token. If a client used STARTTLS and sent a BURL referencing non-public information, the server SHOULD use STARTTLS or an equivalent when fetching it.

The profile adds no further security measures. It notes risks around outband notifications, server and client configuration, proxy servers, intermediaries, OMA deployment models that are not conventional IETF ones, and firewall or mobile-network traversal measures.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed slip must not fall into the wrong hands, so you should carry it in a locked bag (TLS). Even without the bag, the slip is no easier to steal than the whole letter would be.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 4550
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 4550, this document requires more of Lemonade IMAP servers: BINARY, COMPRESS=DEFLATE, CONTEXT=SEARCH, CONTEXT=SORT, CONVERT, ENABLE, ESEARCH, ESORT, I18NLEVEL=1, NOTIFY, QRESYNC, SASL-IR, SORT and URL-PARTIAL, the $SubmitPending and $Submitted keywords, and the CAPABILITY response code. It newly requires Sieve and a list of Sieve extensions of delivery agents, and it recommends DEFLATE for TLS.

Other changes: a new section with requirements on mail user agents (in particular, Format=flowed support), a clarified use of $Forwarded, corrected and extended forward-without-download examples, and a new section on in-band and out-of-band notifications. The RFC says this list might be incomplete.

The IANA section records that this document defines the URL-PARTIAL IMAP capability, which IANA added to its IMAP capability registry.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the new edition of the shopping list. It adds more items for the mailbox keeper and the sorting helper, and it fixes mistakes in the examples.

messages.label: APPEND ... CATENATE
messages.note: Build the new message on the IMAP server from new text plus existing parts.

messages.label: GENURLAUTH
messages.note: Ask for an authorized URL for the assembled message.

messages.label: BURL
messages.note: Give the URL to the submission server instead of the message.

messages.label: URLFETCH
